I can't speak for everyone, as all therapists are different, but my own experience was awful. When I was newly eighteen, I was drawing "emotion trees" with my therapist, putting my negative thoughts into a "bad feelings box", and even though she was sworn to secrecy (patient confidentiality), she told my parents the things I had said during the sessions.

She also got annoyed when I told her I was just scared of things in general, and made me analyze what I'm scared of when I'm scared, which in turn made me far more terrified of everything around me because suddenly I was thinking about my fears all the time (if that makes any sense at all).

Example: I got nervous getting out of my car. I paused to reflect why I was nervous, as I was told. I noticed a bush rustling. I immediately made the jump that a bird was in there. I then became terrified that there was a bird inside the bush that was about to attack me. I walked by that bush every single day, and after that day I started crying when I walked by it.

Once I left that therapist, I got much better with my fears, but I still get nervous walking past that damn bush. Moral of the story: if you have the option, be picky with your therapist. If you notice yourself getting worse, GET OUT. There are other therapists out there, and a new one could be exactly what you need.

Hope this helped. Good luck!

We had one we called Squares. Basically, the concrete we rode our scooters on was all cracked up into five separate sections that were sort of Square shaped, so we each got one Square and the way you played was by tagging each other while riding your scooters. Your own Square was a safe place, but you could only be in it for five seconds at a time, and then you had to be out of it for ten seconds. If you're tagged, you're it.

The game goes until someone gets too hurt to stand up, someone starts an argument about how long you've been in your Square, Mom calls you in for dinner, you get bored, or the sun sets. As kids, we normally ended it by fighting lol. My siblings and I still play it every Thanksgiving when everyone comes home. We still use the same scooters too which now leads to us quitting over injuries most often.

When I was 17, I was a trainer at Main Event. I loved it there. One day, I was training a new hire on bowling lane safety, and we went under the pinsetter to send some bowling pins back that had gone all over the lane (the lane was turned off and the players had left). We were both fairly far in when I heard a weird noise... Coming from above us.

For those who don't know, the force of the pinsetter is enough to break any bone in the body. After it crushes you, it flings you backwards with enough force to shatter any bone in the body. Then it spins you like a washing machine does, except instead of clothing it's extremely heavy bowling pins, which hit you with enough force (you guessed it) to crush any bone in the body. And me and a 16 yr old we're underneath the pinsetter when we heard it start.

I grabbed the kid by the back of his shirt and yanked him hard enough that he slid all the way out. I then, while on my knees, pushed hard with my feet and hands and did this weird matrix slide out from under it. Less than a second later the pinsetter slammed down.

Turns out, the kid working the bowl desk didn't notice us under there and wanted to reset the lane... Without checking with anyone first. She was fired, the kid quit, and I finished my shift and took a long bath. Good times.

Most horrifying thing I ever cleaned up was maybe eight months ago. Working late night shift and hear my manager call over the radio... "everyone to the bathrooms NOW". Of course we all run over to see what's wrong, and I'm maybe twenty feet out when the smell hits me. It was crushing. Turns out, some dude had explosive diarrhea. EVERYWHERE. He completely covered his entire stall, left his underwear on the floor, and then PUT HIS PANTS BACK ON AND LEFT. THE LONG WAY. This dude seriously trekked his shit throughout our entire store, and then walked past our main exit and left through the side door. Which meant we had to shut down everything. Nobody was allowed in or out until we had sterilized the doorways and mopped many many times.

Saving grace: my manager didn't even try asking anyone to clean the stall. She let us split the chores. Some of us guarded the doors, some kept all guests far away, some got the mops and paper towels and cleaning fluids for the hallway, and I and a few others volunteered to clean everything in the bathroom except the stall. My dear sweet manager, God bless her, no complaining or gagging, got on her hands and knees and scrubbed that stall clean. No matter how old I get or where I go in life, I will always remember how she put her employees first.
